name: Shanmukha
definition: Shanmukha is a composite portrait of a thirty-four-year-old Kuruba man working as a truck operator at a limestone quarry near Basavakalyan town in Bidar district, Kalyana Karnataka. He represents the working lives of men in and around this historic temple town who rely on the cement-linked stone economy for their livelihoods, while maintaining deep roots in a community marked by seasonal herding traditions and pride in Basavakalyan's Sharana heritage.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shanmukha drives a tipper truck ferrying limestone from a quarry west of Basavakalyan to a cement plant near Shahabad, making three or four trips a day depending on load times and road conditions. He earns around twelve thousand rupees a month on contract, paid per trip rather than a fixed salary, so a breakdown or a rain closure cuts directly into his income. The quarry is noisy and dusty; he wraps a cloth over his nose and mouth but still coughs through most evenings. Diesel costs, tyre repairs and the occasional bribe to overloading checkpoints eat into what he takes home. He starts before sunrise to beat the heat and the crowded roads, returning by mid-afternoon when the quarry shuts for blasting. On Sundays and festival days he helps his brother tend their small field of jowar and tur on the edge of town, work that feels less pressured but brings in little cash. His wife manages the household budget tightly, stretching every rupee between rent, school fees and groceries. He dreams of owning his own truck one day, though the down-payment for a used vehicle is far beyond his savings.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shanmukha lives with his wife, two sons aged ten and six, and his widowed mother in a rented two-room house in one of Basavakalyan's older neighbourhoods, near the main road to Humnabad. His wife, trained up to seventh standard, stays home to cook, clean and care for his mother, who has joint pain and rarely leaves the house. His elder brother farms the family's ancestral two-acre plot on the town's outskirts and lives there with his own family; the brothers share the harvest but not daily expenses. Shanmukha married at twenty-three, in a simple ceremony arranged by his uncles within the Kuruba community, and his wife brought no dowry beyond clothes and a few gold bangles. He sees his role as provider and his wife's as homemaker, a division neither questions aloud. His mother, widowed young, ran the household when he and his brother were boys, working as a farm labourer; now he insists she rest. His sons are his pride, and he is determined they will finish school and find salaried work, not the dust and uncertainty he has known.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shanmukha studied up to eighth standard at a government Kannada-medium school in Basavakalyan before dropping out to help his brother in the fields after their father's sudden death. He regrets not finishing tenth, knowing it limits his chances for formal employment, but at the time there was no choice. His elder son is in fifth standard and his younger in first, both attending the same government primary school where fees are waived but books, uniforms and noon-meal contributions add up. The school is a fifteen-minute walk from home, manageable for now, but Shanmukha worries about the transition to high school, which will mean either a longer commute or boarding in Bidar if the nearby high school's quality does not improve. He wants his boys to pass SSLC and go on to a diploma or degree, something with a certificate that opens doors. His wife, though less educated, insists they attend every day and helps them with simple homework in the evenings. The idea that his children might work with their hands as he does feels like failure to him; education is the only ladder he can see.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shanmukha's persistent cough, legacy of years breathing quarry dust, has never been formally diagnosed; he takes over-the-counter cough syrup when it worsens but has never visited the government hospital in Bidar for a chest check. His mother's joint pain is treated with balms and occasional paracetamol; a doctor once suggested an X-ray, but the cost and the daylong trip put it off. His wife delivered both sons at the government maternity hospital in Basavakalyan; the first birth was difficult, and she was referred to Bidar, but the second went smoothly. Immunisations for the children are up to date, tracked through the anganwadi, and his younger son recovered quickly from a bout of fever last monsoon. Shanmukha knows men in the quarry who have silicosis—hacking coughs that never stop—and he fears the same fate, but quitting would mean no income. The 108 ambulance is known to everyone, though he has never had to call it. Ayushman Bharat cards were issued to the family two years ago, but he has not used his; he is not sure what it covers or whether the hospital will honour it without hassle.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shanmukha is Kuruba, a Scheduled Caste community with a herding past, though his family has farmed and laboured for two generations and no longer keeps sheep. His neighbourhood is mixed—Kuruba, Madiga, Lingayat and Muslim families side by side—and daily exchanges are cordial, but marriages and temple festivals remain community-bound. He and his family visit the Basaveshwara temple in Basavakalyan town regularly, a site marking the twelfth-century Sharana saint's teaching, and he feels quiet pride that his town holds such a place in Karnataka's history. His mother lights a lamp at home every evening and observes the Kuruba community's festival of Huttari, though it has become modest over the years. Shanmukha does not attend community meetings often—work leaves him too tired—but he contributed money last year when the Kuruba Sangha organised a function at the temple. He sees the Khwaja Bande Nawaz urs procession pass through town each year and respects the tradition, though he does not visit the dargah himself. For him, faith is habit and heritage, not fervour.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Shanmukha holds a ration card, an Aadhaar card and an Ayushman Bharat card, though he is unsure how to use the last one beyond showing it at a hospital counter. His family receives subsidised rice and kerosene through the PDS shop near his house, and his wife collects it monthly without fail. He has not applied for MGNREGA work because the quarry job, insecure as it is, pays better than hundred-day labour. He hears neighbours talk about the Gruha Jyothi scheme reducing electricity bills and his wife mentions that she now travels free on KSRTC buses under Shakti, a small relief when she visits her parents in Humnabad taluk. Shanmukha has never met the gram panchayat president of the revenue village his field falls under, though his brother attends occasional meetings. He does not follow state or national politics closely but knows Basavakalyan's history matters to larger debates about Kalyana Karnataka and the funds the region is supposed to receive; he is sceptical anything will change. Officials, in his experience, ask for papers, make him wait and rarely solve problems. He respects the idea of government schemes but expects little and is rarely disappointed.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shanmukha worries most about his health, knowing the quarry dust is stealing years from his life, and about money—whether his salary will stretch, whether the truck will break down, whether his sons will finish school or be pulled out by circumstance as he was. He is proud of Basavakalyan's place in Sharana history and feels a quiet bond with the town, but he also knows it offers no future for his children beyond the quarry or the fields. He wants his sons to study, find salaried jobs with Saturdays off, and live in a place with cleaner air. He resents that Kalyana Karnataka is labelled backward and yet sees little of the special funds or opportunities he hears mentioned in the news; to him, it feels like the government forgets this region once the speeches are done. He blames no community or person for his struggles, only a vague sense that people like him are expected to manage on their own. What he demands, quietly and without expectation, is that his children get a fair chance—a good school nearby, a hospital that works, a government job if they study hard enough—and that his cough does not become the kind that never stops.
